privacy.title: Your conditions take one sealed path
privacy.intro: Herd separates the service that stores your reply from the private evaluator that checks the group. Here is the whole path.
privacy.flowTitle: From your answer to the event result
privacy.flowPrivacyLabel: Your minimum and required-person conditions are never shown to the host or guests.

flowSteps.title: You answer on your device
flowSteps.body: Your choice, minimum, and required-person conditions are readable here.

flowSteps.title: Your device seals everything
flowSteps.body: Before upload, Herd encrypts and pads the reply into one fixed-size envelope.

flowSteps.title: Herd stores only the sealed reply
flowSteps.body: Herd’s servers store only ciphertext and account-linked delivery metadata. Not even Herd’s own servers can read your reply.

flowSteps.title: A private evaluator returns one result
flowSteps.body: Inside isolated hardware, it checks the group and returns confirmed or not confirmed—and attending members only when confirmed.

sections.title: What’s the layman’s TL;DR?
paragraphs: Your phone or browser locks your full reply before it sends anything. Herd stores the sealed package, but not even Herd’s own servers can read it.

At the deadline, a separate private evaluator checks everyone’s rules together and releases only the event result. Your host and the other guests never receive your minimum or required-person conditions.

sections.title: Who can see my private reply?
paragraphs: You can reopen your latest saved reply on a device that still holds your account secret. The host and other guests cannot read the sealed contents, and not even Herd’s own servers can read them.
The approved confidential evaluator can decrypt replies transiently inside isolated hardware for one purpose: calculate the allowed event result. It does not return the conditions.

sections.title: What information is never shown from my reply?
paragraphs: Your private minimum and required-person conditions are never returned to the host or guests, and not even Herd’s own servers can read them. They are not included in the final result.
Before the deadline, your individual answer is not shown to the group. Herd’s response API and database reject readable answer or condition fields.

sections.title: What information from my reply can be shown?
paragraphs: Everyone can see the final event result: confirmed or not confirmed. If the event is confirmed, the signed result can include the attending members. If it is not confirmed, no individual reply list is released.
Event details, the guest list, and whether you have submitted a response are separate account-linked product data. They are not hidden by the private-response envelope.

sections.title: Can anyone get my condition set?
paragraphs: No. Your host and other guests cannot access your condition set, and not even Herd’s own servers can read it. Only a device holding your account secret can reopen your saved reply for you.

Your phone number signs you into the account, but it is not the decryption key. The approved confidential evaluator briefly opens conditions inside isolated hardware to calculate the result, then returns no condition data. A compromised device can still expose what is visible on that device.

sections.title: What can Herd still learn?
paragraphs: Your submission is account-linked, not anonymous to Herd. Herd can access your phone and profile, event and guest membership, account and invitation IDs, the response slot, frozen policy, ciphertext hash and revision, plus IP, device, timing, delivery, and security metadata.
The SMS provider receives the destination phone number, verification message, and delivery metadata. Encryption protects reply contents; it does not hide account or network metadata.

sections.title: How can I verify the code and release?
paragraphs: Herd publishes its privacy-critical source under the Apache 2.0 license. A deterministic source archive, signed release manifest, software inventory, assembly provenance, deployment statement, and public release pointer bind reviewable source and exact release artifacts into one evidence chain.

The clients verify signed policies, receipts, log entries, evaluator identity, and final results. A monitor can compare served web assets, verify hashes and signatures, and challenge the live evaluator’s hardware attestation.

This makes changes detectable, but it is not the same as an independent audit or a mathematical proof that every delivered client came from the published source. At launch, James administers the cloud projects and monitor; that is disclosed self-custody, not independent governance.

sections.title: What does the private evaluator verify?
paragraphs: Before sending, the client recomputes the frozen event-policy hash, requires the supported protocol and fixed payload size, and requires the evaluator identity embedded in the release. It encrypts the response into an exact envelope; the API rejects legacy or extra readable reply fields.

At evaluation, the confidential workload verifies the committed response batch and frozen policy, applies the group rules, and signs the limited result. iOS and web verify that signature and its event, policy, evaluator, attendee set, and time before displaying a final answer.

sections.title: What if I lose this device?
paragraphs: A fresh phone verification can switch private replies to the current device without requiring another invitation. Herd creates a new private-reply key and a new response on this device can replace the reply previously saved for an active invitation.

The phone code confirms account ownership; it is not the encryption key. Switching signs out other devices, does not recover the previous reply’s contents, and knowingly accepts SIM-swap and recycled-number takeover risk.

sections.title: What can this protection not do?
paragraphs: A compromised device, browser extension with access, screenshot, or someone watching the screen can expose what you see.
Encryption does not hide account and network metadata, prevent service outages, recover an old device key, or turn source publication into an independent audit.
